stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that line $j$ is parallel to line $k$?
stimulus: Ecologists are mapping a restored wetland. Two straight boundary paths, line $j$ and line $k$, are both crossed by a straight drainage ditch, line $t$. Line $t$ meets line $j$ at point $A$ and meets line $k$ at point $B$, with $B$ below $A$. At point $A$, angle 1 is above line $j$ and to the right of line $t$, angle 2 is above line $j$ and to the left of line $t$, and angle 3 is below line $j$ and to the left of line $t$. At point $B$, angle 5 is above line $k$ and to the right of line $t$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Angle 1 and angle 5 are in the same position at the two crossings: above their path and to the right of the ditch. That makes them corresponding angles. If corresponding angles are equal, the lines are parallel, so this fact is enough.

A.why: Angles 1 and 3 are vertical angles at the same crossing, and vertical angles are always equal whenever two lines cross. Because this is true whether or not $j$ and $k$ are parallel, it can't prove that they are.

B.why: Angles 1 and 2 form a linear pair along line $j$, so they always add to $180^\circ$. You used the supplementary rule, but it only proves parallel lines when it applies to same-side interior angles at two different crossings.

D.why: Saying angle 1 equals angle 2 only tells you that each is $90^\circ$, so the ditch is perpendicular to line $j$. It tells you nothing about line $k$, so it doesn't compare the two paths at all.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $ABC$ is similar to triangle $DEF$?
stimulus: A marine biologist divides a kelp survey area into triangular sections. In triangle $ABC$ and triangle $DEF$, $m\angle A = 50^\circ$ and $m\angle D = 50^\circ$, where $A$ corresponds to $D$, $B$ corresponds to $E$, and $C$ corresponds to $F$.
explanation: You already have one pair of equal angles, $\angle A$ and $\angle D$. A second pair, $\angle B = \angle E = 70^\circ$, completes Angle-Angle (AA) similarity.

B.why: For SAS similarity, the equal angle has to sit between the two proportional sides. Sides $AB$ and $BC$ meet at $\angle B$, not at $\angle A$, so this is side-side-angle, which doesn't prove similarity.

C.why: A single pair of equal sides plus a single pair of equal angles doesn't meet any similarity criterion. You still need a second angle or a second proportional side next to the equal angle.

D.why: This is already true because $m\angle D = 50^\circ$ and the angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$. It adds nothing new, so it can't finish a proof.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $PQR$ is congruent to triangle $STU$?
stimulus: At an excavation site, archaeologists stake out two triangular plots, $PQR$ and $STU$, where $P$ corresponds to $S$, $Q$ corresponds to $T$, and $R$ corresponds to $U$. They measure $PQ = ST = 10$ meters and $QR = TU = 7$ meters.
explanation: Angle $Q$ is between sides $PQ$ and $QR$, and angle $T$ is between the matching sides $ST$ and $TU$. Two pairs of equal sides with the equal angle between them is Side-Angle-Side (SAS), so the triangles are congruent.

A.why: Angle $P$ is not between the two known sides, so this is side-side-angle (SSA). Here the side opposite $\angle P$ (7 m) is shorter than the side next to it (10 m), so two different triangles can fit these measurements. SSA isn't a congruence criterion.

C.why: You were reaching for SSS, but this gives the third side of only one triangle. Without knowing that $SU$ is also 12 meters, you can't compare the two plots.

D.why: A right angle in triangle $PQR$ alone says nothing about angle $T$. You'd need to know that triangle $STU$ also has a right angle at $T$ before SAS or HL could apply.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that line $j$ is parallel to line $k$?
stimulus: A printmaker carves two straight grooves, line $j$ and line $k$, into a linoleum block, then cuts a straight line $t$ across both. Line $t$ meets line $j$ at point $A$ and meets line $k$ at point $B$, with $B$ below $A$. At point $A$, angle 2 is above line $j$ and to the left of line $t$, angle 3 is below line $j$ and to the left of line $t$, and angle 4 is below line $j$ and to the right of line $t$. At point $B$, angle 5 is above line $k$ and to the right of line $t$. The measure of angle 4 is $112^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Angles 4 and 5 are both between the two grooves and on the same side of line $t$, so they are same-side interior angles. If $m\angle 5 = 68^\circ$, then $112^\circ + 68^\circ = 180^\circ$. Same-side interior angles that add to $180^\circ$ prove the lines are parallel.

A.why: Angles 2 and 4 are vertical angles at point $A$, so angle 2 is $112^\circ$ no matter how line $k$ is tilted. A fact that is always true can't prove that the lines are parallel.

B.why: Angles 3 and 4 form a linear pair along line $j$, so angle 3 is always $68^\circ$. This involves only one crossing and tells you nothing about line $k$.

C.why: You used the equal-angle rule where the supplementary rule applies. Same-side interior angles must add to $180^\circ$, but $112^\circ + 112^\circ = 224^\circ$, which actually shows the lines are not parallel.

stem: Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle $JKL$ is similar to triangle $MNO$?
stimulus: An immunology poster uses two triangles to show how an antibody's binding arms open. In triangle $JKL$, $JK = 4$ units, $KL = 6$ units, and $JL = 5$ units. In triangle $MNO$, $m\angle N = m\angle K$, where $J$ corresponds to $M$, $K$ corresponds to $N$, and $L$ corresponds to $O$.
explanation: Angle $K$ is between sides $JK$ and $KL$, and angle $N$ is between the matching sides $MN$ and $NO$. Since $\frac{6}{4} = \frac{9}{6} = 1.5$, the sides around the equal angles are proportional. That is SAS similarity.

A.why: The ratios $\frac{6}{4}$ and $\frac{7.5}{5}$ match, but sides $MN$ and $MO$ meet at $\angle M$, not at the equal angle $\angle N$. Proportional sides that don't surround the known angle (SSA) don't prove similarity.

C.why: You added 2 to each side (4 to 6, then 6 to 8) instead of multiplying by the same scale factor. Since $\frac{6}{4} = 1.5$ but $\frac{8}{6} \approx 1.33$, these sides aren't proportional.

D.why: You matched the sides in the wrong order. Comparing $MN$ to $JK$ and $NO$ to $KL$ gives $\frac{9}{4}$ and $\frac{6}{6}$, which aren't equal, so these sides aren't proportional.
